roles: historian of Jewish mysticism and Kabbalah
professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem
summary: Gershom Scholem (1897-1982), born Gerhard Scholem in Berlin and settled in Jerusalem, was the German-born Israeli historian and philologist who founded the modern academic study of Jewish mysticism and Kabbalah and held the first chair in the subject at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. In Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941), Sabbatai Sevi: The Mystical Messiah (Hebrew 1957, English 1973), and essays collected as On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, he advanced, on his own account, the theses that mysticism was a vital and central force in Jewish history rather than a marginal aberration, and reconstructed the history of the Kabbalah philologically from its manuscript sources.
description:
Gershom Scholem, born Gerhard Scholem in Berlin in 1897 into an assimilated German-Jewish family, broke with that milieu as a young Zionist, learned Hebrew and the sources of Jewish tradition, and emigrated to Mandate Palestine in 1923, where he was appointed to the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and became the first professor of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah). He is widely regarded in the scholarship as the founder of the modern, academic, historical-philological study of Jewish mysticism, a field he in large part constituted by gathering, cataloguing, and analyzing the manuscript sources of the Kabbalah. This entry records his scholarly theses as his own attributed positions, the interpretations of a historian, and does not adjudicate them.

Scholem's most widely read work, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism, grew out of lectures delivered in 1938 at the Jewish Theological Seminary in New York and was published in 1941. In it he set out a narrative of Jewish mysticism from the ancient Merkabah (chariot) mysticism through the medieval Kabbalah, the Zohar, the Lurianic Kabbalah of Safed, the Sabbatian movement, and Hasidism. A central thesis, argued as his own scholarly position, was that mysticism had been a living and central force in Jewish religious history, not a marginal or foreign intrusion as an older rationalist historiography (the nineteenth-century Wissenschaft des Judentums) had tended to treat it; on his account the mystical and even the antinomian and messianic currents belonged to the vitality of the tradition and had to be studied on their own terms and from their own sources. This reconstruction, and the value he placed on the material, are recorded here as his attributed interpretation, contested and revised by later scholars, and not endorsed by the editor.

His Sabbatai Sevi: The Mystical Messiah, 1626-1676 (the Hebrew original completed in 1957, the English translation by R. J. Zwi Werblowsky published by Princeton in the Bollingen Series in 1973), is a large-scale study of the seventeenth-century messianic movement gathered around Sabbatai Sevi, which Scholem read as a mass movement generated from within Lurianic Kabbalah and continuing, in clandestine and heretical forms, after Sevi's conversion to Islam; the book is widely counted among his major works. His essays on the symbolic language of the Kabbalah, the doctrine of the sefirot, the tradition of the Golem, and the meaning of the Torah in mysticism were collected in English as On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism. Alongside these he wrote a memoir of his friendship with Walter Benjamin and reflections on Zionism and on German-Jewish history.

Scholem's interpretations were themselves the subject of scholarly debate, which this entry records as debate. He engaged Martin Buber over the reading of Hasidism, arguing in a 1961 critique that Buber's existential retelling did not answer to the historical and textual record, while granting that Buber had brought Hasidism to Western attention; and a later generation of scholars, chief among them Moshe Idel, revised parts of Scholem's synthesis, questioning for instance his account of the place of unio mystica in Jewish mysticism and his broadly historical, as against phenomenological, method. This entry presents Scholem as the modern academic founder of the field on the terms the scholarship uses of him, with his theses attributed to him as scholarly positions and the disagreements about them recorded and not adjudicated.

lifespan.note: 1897-1982 CE. Born Gerhard Scholem in Berlin into an assimilated German-Jewish family; a young Zionist who learned Hebrew and the Jewish sources and emigrated to Mandate Palestine in 1923, where he taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem as the first professor of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah). He died in Jerusalem in 1982.

relations.note: Scholem and Buber were interlocutors; Scholem's 1961 critique ('Martin Buber's Hasidism', Commentary) argued that Buber's existential retelling of Hasidism did not answer to the historical and textual record, while granting that Buber had brought Hasidism to Western attention. Recorded as an attributed scholarly disagreement, not adjudicated (attributed intellectual history). The martin-buber entry exists (data/figures/judaism/martin-buber.json) and records the reciprocal edge; this resolves its dangling forward reference.

Scholem founded the modern academic, historical-philological study of the Kabbalah, reconstructing its history from its manuscript sources; his account of the field is stated as his attributed scholarship, contested and revised by later scholars, not affirmed as metaphysics. The kabbalah entry exists (data/schools/judaism/kabbalah.json).

Scholem treated Hasidism as the last of the major trends in his narrative of Jewish mysticism and engaged Buber over how to read it (see the martin-buber edge); stated as his attributed scholarly position. The hasidism entry exists (data/schools/judaism/hasidism.json).

sources.citation: Biale, David. Gershom Scholem: Kabbalah and Counter-History. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1979 (2nd edition 1982; ISBN 9780674363328; 279 pp.). The standard peer-reviewed monograph on Scholem, the first book devoted to him, treating his founding of the academic study of Jewish mysticism, his conception of Kabbalah as a 'counter-history' recovering the vital and suppressed currents of the tradition, and the place of that project in debates over Zionism and Jewish theology. Cited as the principal academic lens on Scholem himself.
